mainEntity.name: Is northern white cedar as good as western red cedar for a fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: On rot resistance, yes. Both heartwoods are rated durable to very durable, and northern white cedar carries the better insect rating, including resistance to termites and powderpost beetles. Western red cedar is stronger, about 28 percent stiffer, and available in clearer, longer boards, so it is the better choice for rails and gates. For pickets and short spans, white cedar performs well at a lower cost.

Yes. Sapwood has almost none of the extractives that protect heartwood, so it decays like any untreated softwood, especially at the bottom of a picket where soil and leaf litter hold moisture. Look at the end grain before installation: dark core, pale ring. The more pale ring, the shorter that board's life in a wet location.

mainEntity.name: Is cedar-tone the same as cedar?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Cedar-tone is pressure-treated southern yellow pine with iron-oxide pigment infused into the wood under pressure. The preservative, micronized copper azole, provides the rot resistance; the pigment provides the color. It is a legitimate budget fence material and holds fasteners better than cedar, but it is pine and should never be priced or described as cedar.

mainEntity.name: What is the hardest cedar for fence posts?

acceptedAnswer.text: Eastern red cedar, by a wide margin. It rates 900 pounds on the Janka scale against 350 for western red cedar and 320 for northern white cedar, and it is about 43 percent heavier. It is the one cedar routinely used in direct soil contact without treatment, which makes it a strong post material and a poor picket material.

mainEntity.name: Which cedar is best for fence pickets?

acceptedAnswer.text: Western red cedar is the standard for good reason: it is stable, works cleanly, comes in consistent lengths, and takes a finish predictably. Northern white cedar is a solid, less expensive alternative if you accept more knots and more culling. Eastern red cedar is a poor picket choice because of supply, hardness, and movement.

mainEntity.name: How long does a cedar fence last in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A well-built cedar fence with heartwood-heavy boards, posts set below the frost line, and reasonable maintenance typically gives 15 to 25 years in this climate; western red cedar fences past 20 years with only posts replaced are common. Sapwood-heavy boards in wet locations, or shallow footings, will cut that life substantially regardless of species.

mainEntity.name: Should cedar posts be set in concrete?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a privacy fence in Oakland County clay, posts should be set below the 42-inch frost line, and a properly sized concrete footing is the most reliable way to hold them there through freeze-thaw. The footing is not the whole story: the post material, the cut end, and drainage around the base determine how long the post survives. Ground-contact rated material or eastern red cedar is the safer choice in soil.

mainEntity.name: Do I need stainless steel fasteners for a cedar fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: For western red cedar, yes, or a coated alternative rated for exterior use. Iron-based fasteners react with cedar extractives and leave black streaks, particularly when the wood is wet, and the staining is permanent. Stainless costs more up front and is the difference between a fence that ages and a fence that looks damaged.
